trigger: A guard, gate, validator or admission check has just been added or changed, and it passes.
probe: construct an input the gate is SUPPOSED to reject
run it and confirm the gate rejects it, naming the reason
construct an input the gate must NOT reject — the over-firing control — and confirm it passes
if the gate spans more than one code path, repeat per path; do not infer coverage of path B from path A
grep the invariant's SHAPE across the codebase and count the sites; a gate implemented at one of two sites is not a gate
priority: Immediately after any gate change, before believing a green result. A gate that has never rejected anything is indistinguishable from a gate that cannot.

evidence.finding: After a safety net landed forbidding fabricated return values, a closure still built clean and returned a fabricated 0. The invariant was implemented in emit_fn but emit_lambda holds a SECOND site, in a file the implementing agent was forbidden to touch to avoid colliding with parallel work. The diff was correct and complete for every site that agent could see.

The same guard, ported without its non-Unit condition, then OVER-FIRED on statement-bodied closures and broke a codegen parity test. Both directions now pinned: a value-returning closure must refuse, a statement closure must build and agree.
Exited 0 having compared nothing — demonstrated with AXON=/bin/false, which produced '0 match, 0 differ, 42 skipped' and success.

transfers: This is mutation testing's rule applied one level up: mutation asks whether a TEST would notice a broken implementation; this asks whether a GATE would notice a bad input. Neither can be answered by reading the diff, because in both cases the diff is not wrong.
limits: Proves the gate fires on the case you thought of. It says nothing about cases you did not think of, and a gate can still be incomplete in a direction no constructed input reaches.
